descriptionChirho: To writhe or be in anguish, conveying intense physical or emotional pain — Arabic consistently uses تَوَجَّعَ/يَتَوَجَّعُ (tawajjaʿa, Form V of و-ج-ع 'pain'), a distinct root from trembling or labor; Korean uses 고통하다/괴로워하다 (gotong-hada/goerowo-hada, 'to suffer/be distressed'); Swahili uses -umwa/-teseka (passive 'be hurt' / 'suffer'), distinct from -tetemeka 'tremble'; covers all Qal inflections (imperfect, perfect, infinitive, participle) expressing pain and anguish without specific childbirth or trembling connotation.

To tremble, shake, or quake, typically from fear or awe before God — Arabic uses ارْتَعَدَ/يَرْتَعِدُ (irtaʿada, Form VIII of ر-ع-د 'thunder/tremble'), a completely different root from the pain sense; Korean uses 떨다/떨리다 (tteolda/tteollida, 'to tremble/shake'); Swahili uses -tetemeka (intransitive 'tremble'), distinct from -umwa 'be hurt'; the Hifil causative 'make tremble' (يُزَلْزِلُ yuzalzilu, Swahili -tetemsha causative with -sha suffix) and Pual passive 'be made to tremble' are included as causative and passive extensions of this same semantic field.

To be in labor, to travail in childbirth — Arabic uses the specific root تَمَخَّضَ (tamakhaḍa, Form V of م-خ-ض, exclusively 'labor/parturition'), clearly distinguishing this from general pain (تَوَجَّعَ) or trembling (ارْتَعَدَ); Korean uses 해산하다/산고하다 (haesan-hada/sango-hada, 'give birth/have birth pangs'); Swahili uses uchungu wa kuzaa ('pain of bearing') and -pata uchungu ('get labor pain'), with the kuzaa element specifying childbirth; covers Qal forms describing the mother's experience of labor.

Causative-intensive sense: to bring forth, cause to be born, to beget — Arabic uses وَلَدَ (walada, 'give birth') and أَنْجَبَ (anjaba, Form IV causative 'beget'), both from birthing roots distinct from pain or trembling; Korean uses 낳다/탄생시키다 (nata/tanseong-sikida, 'give birth/cause birth') with causative -시키다 morphology; Swahili uses -zalisha (causative of -zaa 'bear' with productive causative suffix -isha) and -umba ('create/form'); the Piel binyan marks intensified/causative action on the birthing sense.

Passive of the birthing sense: to be brought forth, to be born, to be formed — Arabic uses وُلِدَ (wulida, passive of walada 'bear'), تَكَوَّنَ (takawwana, 'be formed'), and صُوِّرَ (ṣuwwira, passive of ṣawwara 'form/shape'), all passive constructions; Korean uses 태어나다/납다 (taeeo-nada/napda, 'be born') and 지어지다 (jieo-jida, passive 'be built/formed'); Swahili consistently uses -zaliwa (passive of -zaa 'bear', with passive suffix -wa); Pual (passive of Piel) and Hofal (passive of Hifil) both express the passive experience of being birthed or formed.

To whirl, swirl, or spin — Arabic uses حَلَّ/يَحُلُّ (ḥalla/yaḥullu, 'descend/alight') and دَارَ/تَدورُ (dāra/tadūru, 'go round/rotate'), roots entirely unrelated to pain, trembling, or birthing; Korean uses 휘몰아치다/돌아가다 (hwimora-chida/dora-gada, 'whirl/go around'); Swahili uses -zunguka ('go around/circle') and -shuka/-anguka ('descend/fall'); the Hitpael participle 'tempest/whirling' (دَائِرَة dāʾira, Korean 휘몰아치는) belongs here as a reflexive-intensive extension of circular motion.

To dance, specifically in a joyful or celebratory context — Arabic uses رَقَصَ (raqaṣa, 'to dance'), a completely distinct root from all other senses; Korean uses 춤추다 (chum-chuda, 'to dance'), a dedicated lexeme with no semantic overlap with pain or trembling; Swahili uses -cheza ('play/dance'), the standard dance verb; the nominal/participial form 'dancers' (الرَّاقِصَات ar-rāqiṣāt, 춤추는 자들 chum-chuneun jadeul, wanawake waliocheza) confirms this as a distinct activity sense.

To wait, to wait patiently, to tarry — Arabic consistently uses انْتَظَرَ (intaẓara, Form VIII of ن-ظ-ر 'look/wait'), a root with zero overlap with pain, trembling, birthing, whirling, or dancing; Korean uses 기다리다 (gidarida, 'to wait'), unambiguous; Swahili uses -ngoja/-ngojea ('wait/wait for') and -ngoja kwa subira ('wait with patience'); the Hitpael form adds reflexive-intensive nuance ('wait upon oneself' → 'wait patiently'), but the core semantics remain 'wait'.

To be wounded, pierced, or struck — Arabic uses جُرِحَ (juriḥa, passive of جَرَحَ jaraḥa 'wound'), from the root ج-ر-ح exclusively meaning physical wounding, not pain in general; Korean uses 두려워하다 (duryeowo-hada, 'fear') and 떨다 (tteolda), showing some semantic blending with trembling in the target language but the Arabic clearly isolates the wounding sense; Swahili uses -teswa (passive causative 'be caused to suffer') and -tetemeka; these occurrences describe being physically struck or wounded rather than writhing in emotional pain.

To rest, settle upon, or extend — Arabic uses امْتَدَّ (imtadda, Form VIII of م-د-د 'extend/stretch'), a unique root among all the senses here, conveying spatial extension or settling; Korean uses 맞다 (matda, 'receive/be hit'), suggesting something alighting or coming to rest; Swahili uses a negated form haikugusa ('did not touch'), implying contact or settling; this rare sense captures the spatial/physical meaning of landing or resting upon something.

A ketiv (written but not read) textual variant — Arabic has أَتَأَلَّمُ (ataʾallamu, Form V of أ-ل-م 'be in pain', first person 'I am in pain'), aligning this with the pain/anguish semantic field; Spanish [me duelo] ('I grieve') confirms this; as a ketiv reading it is a textual note rather than a standalone occurrence but must be assigned; grouped alone because it is a marginal textual apparatus entry rather than a productive verbal form.
